title: Subtraction Within 20 for Grade 1: 4 Smart Strategies + Free Quiz
meta_desc: The four subtraction strategies for Grade 1 within 20 - count back, count up, number bonds and bridging ten - with a free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Some subtractions within 20 are best counted back, others counted up, and 15 − 8 needs a different trick entirely. Here is how to help a Grade 1 child pick the smart strategy, plus a quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Watch a Grade 1 child work out 15 − 13 and you will often see something painful: they hold up fifteen fingers, then fold down thirteen, one at a time, and announce ‘two’ after a long, error-prone struggle. Now watch the same child do 15 − 2. Same fingers, same slow folding. Here is the thing — those two sums have the same answer, but a fluent child solves them two completely different ways. Subtraction within 20 is not one skill. It is a small set of strategies, and the real win in Grade 1 is teaching a child which one to reach for.

This is where subtraction within 20 gets genuinely interesting, because it is the range where numbers cross the ten-line. Once you go past 10 − something, counting on fingers falls apart. Below are the four strategies I actually use with six-year-olds, and, more importantly, when each one is the smart choice.

Why subtraction within 20 needs strategies, not fingers

Addition lets you keep counting up as long as you like. Subtraction is meaner: count the wrong way, or lose your place by one, and the answer is wrong. A child who treats every subtraction the same way — count back on fingers, always — will be slow on the easy ones and hopelessly stuck on the hard ones like 14 − 6. The fix is to notice what kind of subtraction you are looking at before you start.

Strategy 1: Counting back (for small differences)

Counting back is the honest, direct meaning of subtraction: take away. For 17 − 3 you start at 17 and hop back three — 16, 15, 14. Done. This works beautifully when the number you are subtracting is small, say 1, 2 or 3.

The catch, and I see this constantly, is that children start counting back from the wrong place. For 17 − 3 they say ‘seventeen’ as the first hop and land on 15. Teach it as ‘seventeen — then sixteen, fifteen, fourteen’, moving three after seventeen. A number line drawn on paper fixes this faster than any explanation.

Strategy 2: Counting up to find the difference (for close numbers)

Now back to 15 − 13. Counting back thirteen times is madness. But the two numbers are close, so ask a different question: how far apart are they? Start at 13 and count up to 15 — fourteen, fifteen — that is two hops, so the answer is 2. This is finding the difference, and it is the single most under-taught strategy at this age.

The signal to count up is when the two numbers are close together. 18 − 16, 12 − 9, 20 − 17 — all of these are quick as a jump forward and horrible as a count backward. Teaching a child to ask ‘are these numbers close?’ before deciding is worth more than a hundred drilled facts.

Strategy 3: Using number bonds you already know

A child who knows their bonds — the pairs that make ten, and the small facts within ten — gets a whole layer of subtraction for free. If you know 6 + 4 = 10, then 10 − 6 = 4 and 10 − 4 = 6 without any counting at all. The same fact family works for teens: knowing 13 = 10 + 3 makes 13 − 3 = 10 and 13 − 10 = 3 instant.

The fact-family idea

I tell children that a number bond is like a family of four facts that all live together. From 7, 3 and 10 you get 7 + 3, 3 + 7, 10 − 3 and 10 − 7. Learn the family once and subtraction stops being a separate thing you have to memorise. This is the bridge from addition into subtraction, and it is why bonds are worth more practice than anything else in Grade 1.

Strategy 4: Bridging through ten (for crossing the ten-line)

This is the big one, and the reason subtraction within 20 is harder than within 10. Take 15 − 8. You cannot easily count back eight, and the numbers are not close enough to count up quickly. So you bridge through ten: first subtract enough to land on 10, then subtract the rest. 15 − 5 gets you to 10, and you have 3 left to take away, so 10 − 3 = 7. That is 15 − 8 = 7, done in two clean steps.

It leans directly on bonds to ten, which is exactly why strategy 3 comes first. Bridging feels like a stretch at first — model it out loud with a ten-frame and counters for a week before you expect a child to run it alone. When it clicks, the scary teens sums like 14 − 6 and 16 − 9 stop being scary.

Which strategy, and when

The whole point is choosing. Here is the cheat-sheet I wish more classrooms put on the wall.

StrategyBest forExample
Counting backTaking away a small number (1–3)17 − 2
Counting upThe two numbers are close15 − 13
Known number bondsFacts you already know by heart10 − 6
Bridging through tenCrossing the ten-line15 − 8

A quick way to help a child decide, in the order I teach them to ask:

  • Am I taking away just one, two or three? Count back.
  • Are the two numbers close together? Count up to find the gap.
  • Do I already know this as a bond or a fact family? Say the answer.
  • None of those, and it crosses ten? Bridge through ten in two steps.

A realistic way to practise

Ten minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday, and mixed practice matters more than neat rows of the same type. If a worksheet only ever asks 15 − 2, 16 − 3, 14 − 1, the child never learns to choose — they just count back on autopilot. Mix the types on purpose so they have to look at each sum and decide. One honest caveat: do not rush the bridging strategy. A child who is still shaky on bonds to ten will find bridging through ten frustrating, because it is built on top of those bonds. Get the bonds solid first, even if it takes a couple of extra weeks.

Below is a short, free quiz built around exactly these four strategies for subtraction within 20 — counting back, counting up, bonds and bridging ten. quiz.title: Grade 1 Subtraction Within 20 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on subtracting within 20 using counting back, counting up, number bonds and bridging through ten. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is 17 − 2? Count back from the bigger number.
questions.explanation: Counting back is best here because you are taking away a small number. Start at 17 and hop back two: 16, 15.

questions.q: What is 15 − 13? The numbers are close, so which strategy is smart?
questions.explanation: When the two numbers are close, count up to find the difference. From 13 it is two hops to 15, so the answer is 2.
Count up from 13: fourteen, fifteen. That is two hops, so 15 − 13 = 2.
This is a number bond. The family 6, 4, 10 gives you 10 − 6 = 4 with no counting at all.
Bridge through ten: 15 − 5 lands on 10, then take away the leftover 3. 10 − 3 = 7.
Bridge through ten: 14 − 4 gets to 10, then take away the leftover 2. 10 − 2 = 8.

questions.q: Which subtraction is best solved by counting up?
questions.explanation: 18 and 16 are close together, so counting up from 16 to 18 is quick: two hops, difference 2.

questions.q: A child has 13 stickers and gives away 3. How many are left?
questions.explanation: Use the bond: 13 is 10 and 3, so taking away 3 leaves exactly 10. 13 − 3 = 10.

faq.q: What does subtraction within 20 actually cover?
faq.a: Take-away and difference questions where both numbers and the answer stay at 20 or below, including sums that cross the ten-line like 15 − 8. It is the range where a child moves beyond finger-counting into real strategies.

faq.q: When should my child count back and when should they count up?
faq.a: Count back when taking away a small number, such as 17 − 2. Count up when the two numbers are close, such as 15 − 13, where finding the gap is far quicker than hopping backwards.

faq.q: Why is bridging through ten so important?
faq.a: It is the strategy for sums that cross the ten-line, like 14 − 6, which are too big to count back easily. You subtract down to 10 first, then take away the rest — two clean steps instead of one messy one.

faq.q: My child mixes up all the strategies. Is that normal?
faq.a: Completely. Choosing the right strategy is a skill that comes with mixed practice. Keep bonds to ten solid first, then practise sums of different types together so the child has to look and decide rather than count on autopilot.
